new_sources.summary: Abstract Defines forgiveness, and contrasts it with related concepts, namely, to condone, to excuse, to justify, to exonerate, to forget, to atone, and to reconcile, providing concrete examples of each of these. Forgiveness can be an internal, therapeutic process of letting go of anger and resentment, or an interpersonal one of forgoing legal and/or moral claims the victim of an injury has on a perpetrator. The chapter compares and contrasts the views of Judaism and Christianity on whether a victim is morally obligated to forgive a perpetrator when the perpetrator does not repent of his or her misdeed. The trait of “forgivingness” is discussed and the relationship of the tendency to forgive

new_sources.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare and may improve efficiency in clinical support, health management, and doctor-patient communication. Yet its tendency to hallucinate, that is, to generate medical information that appears plausible but is false, can create systemic ethical risks in high-risk medical settings. This paper addresses two questions: what distinctive ethical risks are created by medical AI hallucinations, and what governance mechanisms can respond to them? new_sources.title: Balancing innovation and ethics: responsible governance of artificial intelligence hallucinations in healthcare.
